identity.title: FRABench and UFEval: Unified Fine-grained Evaluation with Task and Aspect Generalization

problem.claim: Evaluate open-ended multimodal large language model outputs across diverse tasks and fine-grained criteria.

gap.claim: Existing evaluators are constrained to specific tasks and aspects, while unified training is hindered by the lack of a large-scale multimodal, aspect-level resource.

contributions.claim: Introduces FRABench, a fine-grained evaluation dataset built from a 112-aspect hierarchical taxonomy, containing 60.4k pairwise samples and 325k labels from human and GPT-4o annotations.
Develops UFEval, a unified fine-grained evaluator spanning natural language generation, image understanding, image generation, and interleaved text-and-image generation.
Reports that aspect-specific learning generalizes to unseen aspects, while joint learning across diverse visual tasks and aspects provides substantial mutual benefits.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe UFEval as the first unified fine-grained evaluator with task and aspect generalization across the four listed evaluation tasks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Authors report that learning specific aspects enables UFEval to generalize to unseen aspects.
Authors report substantial mutual benefits from jointly learning assessment across diverse visual tasks and aspects.
Authors report that FRABench contains 60.4k pairwise samples and 325k evaluation labels obtained through combined human and GPT-4o annotation.

narrative_sequence.summary: Open-ended multimodal output evaluation is presented as a bottleneck amid expanding capabilities, tasks, and modalities.
Existing MLLM-as-a-Judge evaluators are described as task- and aspect-specific.
The paper argues that interconnected criteria may support aspect generalization and that joint task-aspect learning may be synergistic.
The authors introduce a 112-aspect taxonomy and FRABench, then use it to develop UFEval across four evaluation tasks.
Experiments are said to show unseen-aspect generalization and mutual benefits from joint learning.

source_observation.claim: The paper links its evaluator to an explicit aspect taxonomy and reports both cross-aspect and joint-task learning outcomes.

lessons.interpretation: A structured criterion space can make a generalization claim more concrete and connect the resource, method, and evaluation.
lessons.application: Define a hierarchical evaluation taxonomy before training a multi-task evaluator, then separately test transfer to held-out criteria and gains from joint training.
lessons.exception: This may be unsuitable when criteria are not meaningfully related or when held-out aspects cannot be labeled consistently.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the evaluation metrics, baselines, dataset splits, effect sizes, or conditions underlying the reported generalization and mutual benefits.
The claim of being first is attributed to the authors; priority is not independently established.
